title: Tyrannosaurus rex Had Mammal-Like Body Temperature, New Study Reveals (Sci.News)
body:
A fresh look at the fossilized teeth of the iconic Tyrannosaurus rex suggests the Late Cretaceous apex predator was far warmer‑blooded than previously thought, maintaining an internal temperature of roughly 36 °C (97 °F)—a range comparable to modern elephants and significantly higher than that of typical reptiles. The finding, derived from detailed isotopic analysis, adds weight to the growing consensus that many large theropods possessed a metabolic regime closer to that of mammals than to cold‑blooded ancestors.

The research team examined the ratios of oxygen isotopes in the enamel of several well‑preserved T. rex teeth recovered from sites across North America. Because the proportion of heavy oxygen‑18 to light oxygen‑16 in tooth enamel reflects the temperature of the body fluids at the time of formation, scientists can back‑calculate an animal’s core temperature with surprising precision. The results consistently pointed to a narrow thermal window centered around 36.3 °C, with only minor fluctuations that likely correspond to seasonal changes or variations in activity level.

These temperatures sit squarely within the range recorded for large, endothermic mammals such as the African and Indian elephants, which sustain body heat through high metabolic rates and insulating layers of fat and muscle. By contrast, modern reptiles of comparable size—such as large crocodilians—typically exhibit body temperatures that track ambient conditions, often ranging between 20 °C and 30 °C. The implication is that T. rex, despite its reptilian lineage, may have generated and retained heat internally, enabling sustained high‑speed pursuits, rapid growth, and a robust immune response—traits advantageous for a top predator in a dynamic ecosystem.

The study joins a series of recent investigations that have reshaped our view of dinosaur physiology. Earlier work on bone histology, growth rings, and predator–prey ratios hinted at elevated metabolic rates, while analyses of feathered dinosaurs and the discovery of possible warm‑blooded relatives like the small theropod *Velociraptor* have bolstered the argument for endothermy among non‑avian dinosaurs. However, the debate has lingered over whether large theropods were fully endothermic, partially so (mesothermic), or simply benefited from gigantothermy—a phenomenon where massive bodies retain heat passively. The new isotopic evidence leans toward active thermoregulation rather than passive heat retention, suggesting that T. rex possessed physiological mechanisms—perhaps a high‑capacity heart, efficient respiratory system, and specialized insulation—to maintain a stable, elevated body temperature.

Critics caution that isotopic signatures can be influenced by environmental factors such as water sources, diet, and diagenetic alteration of the fossil material over millions of years. The researchers addressed these concerns by selecting teeth from multiple geographic locales and cross‑checking the data against contemporaneous herbivorous dinosaurs, which displayed lower temperature estimates. Nonetheless, the authors acknowledge that further work, including comparisons with other large theropods like *Allosaurus* and *Spinosaurus*, will be essential to confirm whether the warm‑blooded condition was a widespread trait or a unique adaptation of T. rex.

If the findings hold up under scrutiny, they could reshape how paleontologists reconstruct the behavior and ecology of the “king of the dinosaurs.” A higher metabolic rate would imply greater food requirements, potentially influencing herd dynamics of herbivores, migration patterns, and even the frequency of predatory encounters. It may also help explain the rapid growth rates inferred from bone studies, as a sustained internal heat source would accelerate metabolism and tissue development.

Looking ahead, the integration of isotopic chemistry, advanced imaging, and biomechanical modeling promises to unlock further secrets of dinosaur biology. As more specimens are examined and analytical techniques refined, scientists anticipate a clearer picture of how these ancient giants lived, moved, and thrived. The emerging view of T. rex as a warm‑blooded predator not only challenges long‑standing stereotypes but also underscores the complex, nuanced evolution of metabolism across the tree of life.
